To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the metrics are sensitive to speech style and to the degree of foreign accents but are not sensitive to language and dialect.
(1) all the metrics show a considerable degree of variability in the same recordings and (2) the metrics do not correlate with each other.
the global metrics are not reliable in measuring the “speech rhythm” of languages, but they are reliable in measuring the degree of foreign accent of non-native speech.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) the influence of speech rate, 2) the influence of the number of syllables, 3) the influence of local temporal variation, 4) the influence of prominence, 5) the influence of accent, 6) the influence of stress, 7) the influence of intonation, 8) the influence of pauses.

the following: (i) the metrics’ behaviour in the presence of temporal variation in utterance duration and speech rate; (ii) the effect of the number of syllables in an utterance; (iii) the metrics’ sensitivity to the presence or absence of pauses in speech; and (iv) the effect of different speaking styles on the metrics’ values.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the global metrics do not reflect speech rhythm, but they do reflect the temporal distribution of speech segments.
the global rhythm metrics are not reliable enough to be used in research on language or dialect differences.
the metrics are not very useful for the analysis of speech rhythm, but they could serve for other purposes, e.g., for the analysis of temporal variation, and for the study of speech style.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metrics can be successfully used to detect differences between languages, and to some extent, between dialects, speaking registers, and accents.
the global rhythm metrics are not reliable enough to be used as a sole diagnostic tool, but that they can be a useful supplement to other measurements in speech research.
the metrics are sensitive to the presence of pauses, but they are not sensitive to the presence and length of syllables, and they are not sensitive at all to the duration of consonants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global rhythm metrics are not a good measure of the “rhythmic” properties of languages.

the global rhythm metrics are not reliable indicators of speech rhythm, but can be used to quantify the relative durational prominence of syllables in speech, which can be exploited for other purposes.
the global rhythm metrics can be used to detect the presence of speech rhythm but not to measure its strength.
